content: The document titled Guidance for Research Ethics Committees for Rapid Review of Research During Public Health Emergencies was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2020. It addresses the ethical challenges that arise during public health emergencies, such as epidemics and pandemics, and provides specific recommendations for research ethics committees (RECs) to prepare for and conduct rapid reviews of research protocols in such situations. Background Public health emergencies, including epidemics and outbreaks, amplify ethical concerns related to healthcare delivery, privacy, confidentiality, informed consent, community engagement, benefit sharing, and resource allocation. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, no approved treatments or prophylactic products were initially available, similar to previous outbreaks like Ebola, Zika, and Lassa fever. This underscores the critical need for research on new medications and vaccines during pandemics. RECs must be equipped to review such research protocols swiftly and effectively. Countries vary in their readiness to provide ethics reviews for epidemic-related research. Regardless of their level of preparedness, RECs should take proactive steps to prepare for rapid reviews of emergency research protocols. Lessons learned from the 2014 Ebola outbreak have informed the development of ethical guidelines for research during outbreaks. Key issues include balancing the urgency of reviews with the need to maintain quality and protect participants, many of whom may be in dire need of life-saving interventions. Workshops held in 2018, such as those organized by the African Coalition for Epidemic Research, Response, and Training (ALERRT) and WHO, provided recommendations for national and institutional RECs to adapt their standard operating procedures (SOPs) to respond efficiently during pandemics. 1. Parallel Processes: To save time, processes such as drafting, translating, and approving documents should occur simultaneously rather than sequentially. 2. Virtual Meetings: To minimize health risks during infectious outbreaks, RECs should consider virtual meetings and electronic review processes. 3. Language Requirements: Protocols submitted in a language other than the official language of the reviewing country should include key documents (e.g., synopsis, consent forms) in the official language. 4. Checklist for Rapid Review: A checklist should be added to the ethics review form to identify epidemic-related research, describe prior research data, include local investigators, and indicate whether the protocol is part of a multi-center trial. 5. Additional Documentation: Submissions should include collaboration agreements, monitoring and safety plans, data-sharing agreements, and dissemination plans for findings. 6. Rapid Review Process: RECs should establish a process for reviewing protocols as they are submitted, rather than waiting for scheduled meetings. This process should be communicated to researchers. 7. Surge Capacity: RECs should identify members with specialized training in outbreak-related research and recruit additional members as needed to handle increased demand. 8. Quorum Requirements: A quorum for rapid reviews should consist of one-third of the committee members, including relevant experts. 9. Electronic Submissions: Protocols should be submitted electronically to save time, with hard copies provided later if required. 10. Timelines for Review: Protocols should be sent to reviewers within 24 hours of submission, and reviews should be completed within three days. Consolidated feedback should be communicated to the principal investigator within five days. 11. Communication with Investigators: RECs should use electronic or telephonic communication to clarify issues and save time. Investigators should respond to reviews within 48 hours. 12. Documentation: All communications should be documented and archived for future reference. Practical Considerations RECs should pre-identify members who will handle the majority of the review workload and provide them with specialized training. Subject matter experts and individuals with strong ethics knowledge should be contacted in advance to serve as ad hoc members during outbreaks. Additionally, RECs should establish systems for remote discussions, ensuring all members have access to the necessary technology and a backup plan in case of technical issues. Acknowledgments The document acknowledges the contributions of various experts and organizations, including members of the WHO Working Group on Ethics and COVID-19, as well as researchers and ethicists from institutions worldwide.
